actors.name: GE Vernova
actors.role: makes the gas turbines and grid equipment that new data centres need for power
actors.advantage: One of three makers of large gas turbines, with the order book full: a $197bn backlog of equipment and long-term service contracts, 122 GW of gas backlog and slot reservations, and orders up 96% in Q3 2026. A turbine factory takes years to expand, so buyers queue for its output and pay for service for decades.
actors.desire: Turn the power rush into a multi-year backlog at rising prices.
actors.fear: A pause in data-centre building, or cheaper paths to power (solar with storage, small reactors) once its backlog is delivered.

triad.environment: Utilities short of power

actors.name: Siemens Energy
actors.role: Europe's maker of gas turbines and high-voltage grid equipment; the other large-turbine source besides GE Vernova and Mitsubishi Heavy
actors.advantage: It is one of the few firms that can build large gas turbines and grid transformers, so it shares in the same power rush; its edge over GE Vernova is grid technology more than turbine volume.
actors.desire: Win data-centre and grid orders at better margins.
actors.fear: A demand pause, and execution problems of the kind its wind unit had.

actors.name: Vertiv
actors.role: supplies the power distribution and liquid cooling inside AI data centres
actors.advantage: Racks of GPUs need dense power and liquid cooling; Vertiv sells both at scale and designs them alongside NVIDIA's rack generations, so it is specified into most large builds.
actors.desire: Be designed into each new GPU generation's racks.
actors.fear: A capex pause, and rivals such as Schneider Electric and Eaton.

actors.name: Constellation
actors.role: the largest US nuclear operator, selling around-the-clock carbon-free power to data-centre buyers
actors.advantage: Existing nuclear plants are the scarcest firm, clean power, and new reactors take a decade to build. Constellation owns the largest fleet and signs 20-year contracts with hyperscalers.
actors.desire: Sign long contracts at premium prices for its reactors.
actors.fear: Regulators limiting data centres beside reactors; a demand pause.

actors.name: NextEra
actors.role: the largest US developer of wind, solar and storage, and Florida's regulated utility
actors.advantage: Development scale and a regulated utility's cheap capital let it add power fastest where the grid allows; it sells data centres new renewable and storage capacity.
actors.desire: Sell gigawatts of new power to data centres.
actors.fear: Grid interconnection queues, higher interest rates and subsidy cuts.

actors.name: ASML
actors.role: the only maker of extreme-ultraviolet lithography machines
actors.advantage: No rival makes EUV systems. Every leading-edge fab at TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix and Micron queues for the same machines, and ASML says its planned supply for 2027 and 2028 will not meet demand.
actors.desire: Raise capacity as fast as its supplier base allows and keep the lead into High-NA.
actors.fear: Export rules that cut China, a capex pause by customers, and a slow second-source such as nanoimprint or a Chinese EUV effort.

triad.information: Decades of accumulated optics, light-source and software know-how and a supplier web around Zeiss and Cymer
triad.execution: Ships machines that no one else can build, on a schedule customers plan their fabs around
triad.environment: Dutch and US export rules decide which fabs may buy

actors.name: Applied Mat.
actors.role: the largest maker of chipmaking equipment (deposition, etch, inspection)
actors.advantage: The broadest tool line in the industry and an installed base whose service and upgrades tie fabs to it; rivals match it tool by tool but not across the line.
actors.desire: Gain from gate-all-around transistors, backside power and advanced packaging.
actors.fear: Export limits on China and a capex pause by chipmakers.

actors.name: Lam Research
actors.role: leads etch and deposition tools, critical for memory and 3D structures
actors.advantage: Process know-how in high-aspect-ratio etch, which 3D NAND, DRAM and stacked HBM depend on; memory makers design around its tools.
actors.desire: Ride the memory build-out.
actors.fear: China limits and the end of the memory boom.

actors.name: Tokyo Electron
actors.role: Japan's chip-tool leader; its coater-developers run beside every lithography scanner
actors.advantage: A near-monopoly in the coater-developer tracks paired with EUV scanners, plus strong etch and deposition lines.
actors.desire: Hold the track monopoly into High-NA EUV.
actors.fear: Export alignment with US rules and a capex pause.

actors.name: KLA
actors.role: dominates process control: the inspection and metrology that find defects on wafers
actors.advantage: Yield at advanced nodes depends on finding defects early; KLA's inspection tools and their data libraries have no close rival.
actors.desire: Grow with every new node and packaging step.
actors.fear: China limits and a capex pause.

actors.name: Synopsys
actors.role: chip-design software (EDA) and IP; with Cadence it designs nearly every advanced chip
actors.advantage: Design flows, verified libraries and engineers trained on its tools make switching costly. The EDA duopoly is a quiet choke point that US rules can switch off for China.
actors.desire: Sell AI-driven design tools to every chip team.
actors.fear: Export rules cutting China, and customers' in-house tools.

actors.name: Cadence
actors.role: chip-design software and system simulation; Synopsys's duopoly partner
actors.advantage: Lock-in through design flows and engineers' training, shared with Synopsys; strong in analog, packaging and system simulation.
actors.desire: Sell design and simulation to every AI chip team.
actors.fear: Export rules cutting China.

actors.name: Arm
actors.role: licenses the instruction set behind nearly all phones and a growing share of data-centre CPUs (NVIDIA Grace, AWS Graviton, Google Axion)
actors.advantage: Network economies: the software ecosystem built for Arm makes it the default alternative to x86, and it earns royalties on every chip without making any.
actors.desire: Raise royalties as its designs move into AI data centres.
actors.fear: RISC-V, and licensees designing around it.

actors.name: TSMC
actors.role: makes the leading-edge chips (and packages the largest accelerators) for NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom's customers and Apple
actors.advantage: A pure-play foundry that out-executed Samsung and Intel on every recent node. Customers co-design with it, so it holds a record share of foundry revenue and fully booked 3nm and 5nm capacity. Its margin stays high even while it spends heavily.
actors.desire: Be the only place every advanced chip is made, and ration its capacity at rising prices.
actors.fear: A Taiwan Strait crisis, tool inflation and EUV supply, a customer that moves to Intel or Samsung, and losing the favour of Washington.

triad.information: Years of yield learning at each node that a rival cannot buy
triad.execution: Pure-play model: it never competes with its customers, so they hand it their designs
triad.environment: Taiwan: concentration of the world's leading-edge capacity on one island

actors.name: Samsung
actors.role: the largest memory maker and the second-ranked foundry; HBM challenger
actors.advantage: Largest DRAM scale and the one HBM supplier able to add large capacity quickly. Its HBM share jumped as HBM4 ramped. Its foundry arm trails TSMC badly.
actors.desire: Take back HBM leadership and prove its foundry.
actors.fear: Staying second in both memory logic and foundry; Chinese DRAM (CXMT) at the low end.

triad.information: Everything from memory to logic under one roof
triad.execution: Lost HBM3E qualification time, regained share with HBM4
triad.environment: Home market capital and a captive demand base

actors.name: Intel
actors.role: the American fab trying to become the second source to TSMC
actors.advantage: Mostly political and strategic: it is the one US leading-edge fab, so Washington and its rivals' customers want it to survive. NVIDIA completed a $5 billion investment in it.
actors.desire: Win an external foundry customer at 14A.
actors.fear: Being a customer-less fab; running out of capital before a customer commits.

triad.information: Legacy of x86 and process know-how
triad.execution: Lost the lead in the 2010s; rebuilding with 18A and 14A
triad.environment: Backed by the US government and by NVIDIA, which invested to keep a domestic alternative to Taiwan

actors.name: SMIC
actors.role: China's leading foundry; it makes Huawei's Ascend chips without EUV
actors.advantage: State backing and a protected home market. It reaches 7nm-class chips with older DUV tools by multi-patterning, at lower yield and higher cost, and ranks third in foundry revenue.
actors.desire: Reach 5nm-class production without EUV.
actors.fear: Tighter tool controls, including the servicing of the DUV tools it has.

triad.environment: State capital and a protected market

actors.name: SK Hynix
actors.role: the leading maker of high-bandwidth memory, which is stacked beside every NVIDIA accelerator
actors.advantage: It moved first on HBM, qualified with NVIDIA, and now sells out through 2029. Its operating margin (about 80%) is higher than NVIDIA's, which shows the scarce input has become the best business in the chain.
actors.desire: Turn an HBM lead into long-term contracts before Samsung catches up.
actors.fear: Samsung's HBM4 recovery, a cyclical memory downturn, and customers that integrate (Google, Amazon) or push prices back.

triad.information: Early HBM bet and qualification history with NVIDIA
triad.execution: Yields on stacked memory and early HBM4 shipments
triad.environment: Long-term agreements covering over half of 2027-28 capacity and a memory shortage

actors.name: Micron
actors.role: the only US memory maker; third in HBM
actors.advantage: A scarce input at a time of shortage: its gross margin reached 86.8% and revenue went from $11.32 billion to $54.23 billion in a year, but its HBM share slipped.
actors.desire: Hold HBM share and lock multi-year prices.
actors.fear: Share loss to Samsung and the end of the shortage.

triad.execution: Booked most of its 2027 HBM supply
triad.environment: US support for domestic memory

actors.name: CXMT
actors.role: China's largest DRAM maker, listed in Shanghai (688825.SS)
actors.advantage: State-backed scale in commodity DRAM inside China's protected market, and an HBM programme to supply Huawei. Its edge is environment (subsidy and a closed market) more than technology.
actors.desire: Supply China's AI chips with domestic memory, including HBM.
actors.fear: US controls on memory tools and a DRAM price collapse.

actors.name: NVIDIA
actors.role: designs the accelerators, networking and software that nearly every frontier model is trained and served on
actors.advantage: CUDA and the NVLink and networking stack make each model, library and engineer a sunk cost, so buyers pay a gross margin no merchant chip company has held before. It is also the biggest single buyer of memory and packaging, so it can buy the scarce inputs first.
actors.desire: Make compute the unit of the economy: 'compute is revenue' (Jensen Huang, Aug 2026), and keep customers able to afford more of it by financing their land, power and capacity.
actors.fear: A hyperscaler or lab that stops buying at the margin (half its revenue is hyperscale), a cheaper accelerator that runs frontier models without CUDA, Taiwan, and an export regime that closes China for good.

triad.information: Two decades of GPU and CUDA know-how, plus first sight of every lab's roadmap because every lab is a customer
triad.execution: Annual product cadence (Blackwell Ultra now shipping, Vera Rubin in production) and the ability to lock up scarce supply years ahead
triad.environment: Sits between the capital of the hyperscalers and the capacity of TSMC and the memory makers; the US government decides where it may sell

actors.name: AMD
actors.role: the merchant alternative to NVIDIA, with the Instinct accelerators and EPYC CPUs
actors.advantage: It is the only merchant accelerator with the scale to be a second source. Buyers back it to hold NVIDIA's pricing. Its data-center segment nearly doubled in a year but its gross margin is far below NVIDIA's.
actors.desire: Win a double-digit share of AI accelerators with rack-scale systems.
actors.fear: ROCm still trailing CUDA, and the same TSMC and HBM supply constraints as NVIDIA but less priority.

triad.information: Rack-scale (Helios) design now matched to NVIDIA's
triad.environment: Customers want a second source: Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and Oracle run workloads on Helios

actors.name: Broadcom
actors.role: designs custom AI accelerators (Google's TPU) and AI networking for the hyperscalers
actors.advantage: The hyperscalers' path round NVIDIA. It designs the TPU and the networking and has contracts to supply Google's TPUs through 2031, including capacity for Anthropic.
actors.desire: Be the default design house for every hyperscaler's custom silicon.
actors.fear: Customers insourcing design, and a hyperscaler capex cut.

triad.execution: Delivers racks and networking to a cadence the hyperscalers cannot match in-house
triad.environment: Hyperscalers want to escape the NVIDIA margin

actors.name: Huawei
actors.advantage: A captive market and a full stack: Ascend chips, CANN software, and DeepSeek's V4 tuned to them. Policy shields it from NVIDIA; SMIC's output and HBM supply limit how much it can ship.
actors.role: China's leading domestic AI accelerator maker (Ascend), built at SMIC
actors.desire: Replace NVIDIA inside China.
actors.fear: Supply: SMIC cannot make enough chips, and it lacks EUV and HBM supply.

triad.information: Full-stack from chip to model host
triad.execution: Output limited by SMIC yield and cycle time
triad.environment: Protected domestic market as Beijing blocks NVIDIA H200 and Washington blocks the best chips

actors.name: Marvell
actors.role: designs custom AI chips for hyperscalers (AWS Trainium) and the optical links between accelerators
actors.advantage: Custom-silicon and electro-optics design teams for hyperscalers that want an alternative to Broadcom; a second design house rather than a platform.
actors.desire: Win more custom accelerator programmes.
actors.fear: Losing a programme to Broadcom or to in-house teams.

actors.name: Arista
actors.role: Ethernet switches for AI clusters
actors.advantage: High-speed Ethernet switching with software (EOS) trusted by Microsoft and Meta; Ethernet is displacing InfiniBand in many AI clusters.
actors.desire: Make Ethernet the fabric of AI.
actors.fear: NVIDIA's own Ethernet (Spectrum-X) and customers building white-box switches.

actors.name: Dell
actors.role: builds AI servers and racks for enterprises, GPU clouds and xAI
actors.advantage: Scale in server supply chains and enterprise sales; it resells NVIDIA's systems and keeps a thin margin of its own.
actors.desire: Be the enterprise's AI-factory vendor.
actors.fear: NVIDIA and the ODMs selling direct; thin margins.

actors.name: Foxconn
actors.role: assembles NVIDIA's rack-scale AI servers and Apple's iPhones: the world's largest electronics manufacturer
actors.advantage: Process power and scale in assembly; it builds NVIDIA's GB200 and GB300 racks at volume, but on thin margins set by its customers.
actors.desire: Move up from assembly to whole AI data-centre systems.
actors.fear: Customers moving assembly to rivals or to other countries; tariffs.

actors.name: Microsoft
actors.advantage: Microsoft owns the enterprise channel (Microsoft 365, Azure) and about 27 percent of OpenAI, and also sells Anthropic's Claude. Microsoft Cloud earns $63.9bn a quarter, and it funds about $170bn a year of capex while staying cash-flow positive.
actors.role: Azure, OpenAI's early backer, reseller of Claude
actors.desire: Keep Azure the default enterprise AI cloud
actors.fear: Spending $170bn a year on capacity that demand does not fill

triad.environment: Azure capacity

actors.name: Amazon
actors.advantage: Two scale businesses: the largest e-commerce logistics network (more than 1.5 billion items delivered same-day or overnight in one quarter) and the largest cloud (AWS, $46.0bn a quarter, growing 39%), with its own Trainium chips to which Anthropic committed $100bn over ten years. Each funds the other, and rivals must match both.
actors.role: AWS, Trainium chips, backer and host of Anthropic and OpenAI
actors.desire: Be the cloud under every lab
actors.fear: Free cash flow turning deeply negative

triad.environment: Capital and logistics

actors.name: Alphabet
actors.role: TPU chips, Cloud, Gemini and DeepMind
actors.advantage: Alphabet is the only large player with models, chips, cloud and distribution in one company. Google Cloud revenue doubled in the latest quarter and Anthropic buys its TPUs, so Google earns from a rival's growth.
actors.desire: Own the full stack and monetise through Cloud
actors.fear: Capex outrunning cash flow; Pichai: no company would be immune if the boom bursts

triad.information: DeepMind research; the transformer paper came from Google
triad.environment: Search and Android distribution

actors.name: Meta
actors.role: Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp; funds its own AI data centres, chips (MTIA) and Superintelligence Labs from advertising
actors.advantage: Meta funds the build-out from an advertising business ($64.6bn of revenue a quarter) and buys talent outright: $14.3bn into Scale AI and packages reported up to $300m. Its chief says he would rather misspend hundreds of billions than be late.
actors.desire: Superintelligence first
actors.fear: Being late to it

triad.environment: Advertising cash flow

actors.name: Oracle
actors.advantage: Oracle's durable base is its database and enterprise applications, which customers rarely leave because their systems are built on them. On that cash flow it bet on building OpenAI's Stargate capacity to order: $664bn of booked backlog, much of it one customer's $300bn contract, and $28.5bn of capex in one quarter, so its new advantage is also its risk.
actors.role: builds OpenAI's Stargate capacity; largest backlog per revenue
actors.desire: Become a top-three cloud
actors.fear: Funding gap and a single large customer

triad.environment: Willingness to take debt

actors.name: CoreWeave
actors.role: the largest independent GPU cloud, renting NVIDIA capacity to Microsoft, OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic
actors.advantage: CoreWeave turned early NVIDIA allocation into long rental contracts and a backlog near $100bn. But it borrowed about $35.1bn against those contracts and is valued at only $25.59bn: speed without a lasting moat.
actors.desire: Stay the neutral GPU landlord and refinance cheaply.
actors.fear: A customer that cuts or delays, rising debt costs, and GPUs that age before they pay back.

triad.environment: Contracts with OpenAI

actors.name: Alibaba
actors.role: China's largest cloud and the maker of Qwen, a leading open-weight model family; also China's largest e-commerce group
actors.advantage: Alibaba Cloud is China's largest, its open Qwen models spread its platform, and it buys Huawei's chips where NVIDIA's are barred. Its position rests on China's protected market.
actors.desire: Lead China's AI cloud and models.
actors.fear: Chip supply, and price wars with ByteDance and Tencent.

actors.name: OpenAI
actors.advantage: ChatGPT is the default consumer AI brand: more than 900 million weekly users, over 50 million subscribers and 55.5% of chatbot web traffic in August 2026, down from 73.3% in summer 2025 as Gemini and Claude grew. OpenAI turned that audience into the largest private compute buyer, with contracts at Microsoft, Oracle, AWS, CoreWeave, NVIDIA, AMD and Broadcom. The advantage is real but financed: revenue must keep growing to pay the commitments.
actors.role: trains ChatGPT and frontier models; buys compute from every cloud
actors.desire: Be the default intelligence layer and win the compute race
actors.fear: That a growth miss strands commitments it cannot pay

triad.information: Scaling insight and a deep research bench
triad.execution: Fastest consumer product ramp (900M weekly users)
triad.environment: Capital from Amazon, NVIDIA, SoftBank and Microsoft

actors.name: Anthropic
actors.advantage: Anthropic grew its run-rate from about $9bn to over $47bn in five months by selling to enterprises and developers (over 1,000 customers each spend $1m a year), and buys compute on three chip platforms from Google, Amazon, Microsoft and xAI so no single supplier holds it. Its edge is revenue quality and a hedged compute plan.
actors.role: trains Claude, strongest in enterprise and coding; multi-cloud
actors.desire: Frontier model leadership with revenue to match
actors.fear: Over-buying compute by a year and going bankrupt (its CEO's words)

triad.information: Alignment and interpretability research; talent from OpenAI
triad.execution: Enterprise and Claude Code distribution; capacity bought in step with revenue
triad.environment: Only frontier model on all three big clouds

commitments.period: as of the S-1 (mid-2026), lower bound

actors.name: xAI
actors.role: Grok and the Colossus data centres; merged into SpaceX in 2026
actors.advantage: xAI's advantage is speed of building and a rich parent. It also rents Colossus capacity to a rival lab for $1.25bn a month, which turns a model competitor into a landlord.
actors.desire: Catch the lead labs
actors.fear: Burning cash faster than the parent can fund

triad.execution: Builds data centres fast in Tennessee
triad.environment: Capital and cross-subsidy from SpaceX

actors.name: DeepSeek
actors.role: China's leading open-weight model lab, owned and funded by the hedge fund High-Flyer
actors.advantage: It releases near-frontier models free under the MIT licence, trained and served cheaply, and tuned its V4 to Huawei's Ascend chips. Its counter-position is price: closed labs must justify charging for what DeepSeek gives away.
actors.desire: Frontier capability at a fraction of the cost, and a public listing.
actors.fear: Compute limits from export controls, and rivals closing access after distillation accusations.

actors.name: Apple
actors.role: sells the devices through which most consumers meet AI, and the services layer on top of them
actors.advantage: An installed base locked into one ecosystem (switching costs) and a brand that carries a premium price; Services then earns on that base without the cost of building the hardware again. Rivals can make a phone but not copy the base. It is the largest company on the scoreboard.
actors.desire: to keep the device and Services flywheel growing: its CEO calls the year its best fiscal year ever
actors.fear: that the AI interface moves to someone else's model or device and the base stops being the gate; and that tariffs return

triad.information: owns the customer relationship and the usage data of its device base
triad.execution: designs hardware and software together and has others build and supply them at scale
triad.environment: US consumer and tariff policy: a tariff refund added about a point to its Q4 gross margin

actors.name: SpaceX
actors.role: rockets (the lowest cost to orbit), the Starlink satellite network and, since 2026, xAI; listed in June 2026
actors.advantage: A reusable launch system gives the lowest cost to orbit; that cost lets it build a satellite network, and the listing gives it capital to follow into AI. The market values it at $1.823 trillion. Tesla holds a stake in it.
actors.desire: to extend the launch advantage into a space-and-AI conglomerate
actors.fear: an IPO valuation that assumes growth it cannot deliver, and loss of government favour

triad.environment: capital markets let it list at a value above $2 trillion on day one, and US government contracts

actors.name: Palantir
actors.role: sells AI software (AIP, Foundry, Gotham) that governments and companies run on their own data
actors.advantage: Deployments embedded in defence and enterprise operations create high switching costs, and its security clearances are hard for rivals to obtain. The market prices it for perfection.
actors.desire: Be the operating system for AI in government and industry.
actors.fear: Budget cuts, a de-rating, and model makers moving into its niche.

actors.name: Tencent
actors.role: China's largest social, games and payment platform; spending heavily on AI compute
actors.advantage: WeChat's network gives it distribution for any AI product; Q2 2026 revenue rose 11% (US$30.36 billion) while it stepped up compute purchases and profit rose only 0.7%. Its fear is the chip supply.
actors.desire: to convert usage of its apps and models into revenue, in its own words
actors.fear: not being able to buy enough compute, and a slowdown in advertising

triad.information: the data of a very large number of WeChat users
triad.execution: ships AI features into an app everyone already uses
triad.environment: China's regulation and export controls on chips

actors.name: Consumers
actors.role: households that buy devices, subscriptions, medicines and goods, and whose attention advertisers buy
actors.advantage: Not a firm: the final source of most revenue in the chain. Its power is choice, which network effects and switching costs restrain.
actors.desire: Better products for less.
actors.fear: Inflation, job loss and higher energy bills.

actors.name: Enterprises
actors.role: companies that buy cloud, AI and advertising, including the AI natives, utilities and developers that buy chips and power
actors.advantage: Not a firm: the business demand on which the clouds' revenue rests.
actors.desire: Productivity from AI at falling cost.
actors.fear: Paying for AI that does not pay back.

actors.name: Governments
actors.role: public buyers of AI software, defence systems and sovereign AI clusters
actors.advantage: Not a firm: a buyer whose orders follow security and policy rather than price.
actors.desire: Sovereign AI capability.
actors.fear: Dependence on foreign suppliers.

actors.name: SoftBank
actors.role: Stargate chair, OpenAI's largest outside investor
actors.advantage: SoftBank has put $64.6bn into OpenAI and chairs Stargate. It buys position by capital alone.
actors.desire: Own the intelligence layer through OpenAI
actors.fear: A leveraged balance sheet if OpenAI falters

triad.environment: Access to Japanese and Gulf capital

actors.name: Venture funds
actors.role: the venture, growth and sovereign funds that finance private AI labs
actors.advantage: Not a firm: the risk capital of an open economy. In 2026 it is one bet: AI took 82.7% of a record $515.8bn of US venture deal value.
actors.desire: Back the next winner.
actors.fear: A closed exit window and marks that fall.

actors.name: JPMorgan
actors.role: the largest US bank; the plumbing through which AI-era capital raising and trading passes
actors.advantage: Balance-sheet scale and the deposit base lower its cost of funds; being the dealer in the biggest capital raisings gives it fees from the AI financing boom. A bank's rivals are regulation and its own credit losses more than other banks.
actors.desire: to be the bank every large capital raising and payment flows through
actors.fear: a credit event in the loans and bonds that fund the AI build, and rules that cap its balance sheet

triad.information: sees payments, lending and trading flows across the economy
triad.execution: runs consumer, investment-banking and markets businesses at scale
triad.environment: gains when rates are high and capital markets are busy

actors.name: Berkshire
actors.role: a holding company that turns insurance float and cash flow into ownership of other firms; the economy's patient buyer
actors.advantage: Cheap, sticky capital (insurance float) plus the ability to wait. Its advantage is the option to buy when others must sell. A cash pile of $365.5 billion is a weapon in a crisis and a drag in a boom; in 2026 the new CEO began to spend it.
actors.desire: to buy great businesses at fair prices when fear makes them cheap
actors.fear: a permanent loss of capital and a market in which nothing is cheap enough to buy

triad.information: decades of capital-allocation judgement that now passes from Buffett to Abel
triad.execution: buys whole businesses and leaves operators alone; keeps a very large cash buffer
triad.environment: its cash earns interest at 3.75 to 4.00 percent funds-rate levels while it waits

actors.name: US government
actors.role: the rule of law, the patent system, export controls and the dollar; through the Federal Reserve, the price of money
actors.advantage: It sets the environment the chain stands on: courts and patents, deep capital markets, export licences that decide who abroad may buy advanced chips and tools, and a 9.9% stake in Intel. The Federal Reserve held rates at 3.75-4% in October 2026, with two members wanting a rise.
actors.desire: AI leadership over China, chip making at home, and growth without inflation.
actors.fear: Losing the AI race, a Taiwan crisis, and inflation from oil and tariffs.

triad.environment: capital markets

actors.name: China
actors.role: the second AI power, with its own chip, model and demand base
actors.advantage: It can close its own market and order its firms to buy domestic.
actors.desire: Self-sufficiency in AI compute.
actors.fear: Dependence on foreign tools and Taiwan's fabs.

triad.information: Own models (DeepSeek, Alibaba) running on domestic chips
triad.execution: Industrial policy: blocked NVIDIA to nurture Huawei
triad.environment: Largest manufacturing base but cut off from EUV and top-end chips

actors.name: Taiwan
actors.role: home of TSMC's leading-edge fabs: the single place where most advanced chips are made
actors.advantage: It hosts most of the world's advanced chip making, a 'silicon shield' that gives the US and others a stake in its security.
actors.desire: Stay indispensable.
actors.fear: A blockade or attack from China.

actors.name: EU
actors.role: the single market and its regulators (the AI Act, competition law); home of ASML's supply base
actors.advantage: Market size and rule-making: firms everywhere adapt to its rules, but it has few AI champions of its own.
actors.desire: Sovereign AI and chip capacity.
actors.fear: Dependence on US clouds and Asian fabs.

actors.name: Netherlands
actors.role: home of ASML; its export licences decide which lithography tools reach China
actors.advantage: It holds the licence over the one EUV maker, so it is a lever in US-China technology policy.
actors.desire: Keep ASML at home and its trade open.
actors.fear: Being squeezed between Washington and Beijing.

actors.name: South Korea
actors.role: home of SK Hynix and Samsung: most of the world's high-bandwidth memory
actors.advantage: It holds most HBM capacity, so every AI accelerator depends on its fabs.
actors.desire: Keep the memory lead and build foundry share.
actors.fear: China's memory makers, and US-China decoupling squeezing its exports.

actors.name: Japan
actors.role: home of Tokyo Electron, SoftBank and key chip materials such as photoresists and wafers
actors.advantage: Near-monopolies in chip materials and coater-developer tools; it backs a new leading-edge foundry (Rapidus).
actors.desire: Rebuild a leading-edge chip industry.
actors.fear: Dependence on Taiwan and an older, shrinking workforce.

triad.environment: cheap capital

actors.name: Gulf states
actors.role: oil exporters and sovereign investors (Aramco, MGX); the Strait of Hormuz runs past them

flashpoints.title: CUDA against the second sources
flashpoints.mechanism: Every framework, library and engineer is tuned to CUDA, so AMD and the TPU win only where a buyer can rewrite its stack and wants a second source.
flashpoints.outcome: NVIDIA keeps about 75% of accelerators, down from about 87% in 2024, while AMD's data-centre revenue reached a record $8.5bn and Broadcom's AI revenue $16.7bn in a quarter.

flashpoints.title: The TPU bypass
flashpoints.advantage: its own chip, designed with Broadcom
flashpoints.mechanism: A hyperscaler that owns its workloads designs its own accelerator with Broadcom and sells the capacity, avoiding NVIDIA's margin in a way NVIDIA cannot answer without cutting it.
flashpoints.outcome: Just over half of Google's ML compute goes to TPUs, with 4.3 million TPU shipments projected for 2026, and Anthropic took 3.5 GW of Broadcom-built TPU capacity from 2027 plus 5 GW from Google Cloud.

flashpoints.title: AMD buys its way in
flashpoints.mechanism: Buyers who want a second source take AMD's MI450 on large commitments, and AMD pays for the switch with warrants and lower margins.
flashpoints.outcome: OpenAI committed 6 GW with warrants for up to 160m AMD shares, Meta 6 GW in an estimated $60bn deal, and AMD's data-centre revenue rose 97% to $8.5bn in Q3 2026.

flashpoints.title: Memory earns more than NVIDIA
flashpoints.advantage: the scarcest input, sold out to 2029
flashpoints.mechanism: HBM capacity could not grow as fast as accelerators, so memory makers sold out for years and NVIDIA committed capital to secure supply.
flashpoints.outcome: SK Hynix's operating profit was 83.33 of 104.6 trillion won of revenue (about 80%), above NVIDIA's 66%, and NVIDIA's purchase commitments rose from $119bn to $279bn.

flashpoints.title: HBM: SK Hynix against Samsung
flashpoints.mechanism: SK Hynix qualified its HBM with NVIDIA first and locked in long contracts, while Samsung used its larger DRAM capacity to catch up as HBM4 ramped.
flashpoints.outcome: SK Hynix held 50% of HBM in Q2 2026, down from 64% a year earlier, while Samsung rose from 21% to 33% in one quarter and Micron held 18%.

flashpoints.title: EUV: one machine, one maker
flashpoints.mechanism: Only ASML can build EUV systems, so every leading-edge fab must buy from it, and export rules can switch China off.
flashpoints.outcome: ASML reported record Q3 2026 net sales of EUR 11.7bn and says supply for 2027 and 2028 will not meet demand, while China buys only older DUV tools.

flashpoints.title: TSMC against Intel and Samsung
flashpoints.advantage: yield at the leading edge, and trust
flashpoints.mechanism: Customers design for TSMC first because only it delivers leading-edge yield at volume, and as a pure foundry it never competes with them.
flashpoints.outcome: TSMC took 72.5% of top-10 foundry revenue in Q2 2026 against Samsung's 5.9% and SMIC's 5.4%, with a 66.4% gross margin, while Intel needed the US government (9.9%) and NVIDIA ($5bn) as owners.

flashpoints.title: China shuts NVIDIA out
flashpoints.advantage: state control of a large market
flashpoints.mechanism: After Washington allowed H200 sales, Beijing told customs to block them and steered its firms to Huawei's Ascend, so its market became a protected home for its own chips.
flashpoints.outcome: NVIDIA's China share fell to zero by its CEO's account and its guidance assumes no China data-centre compute, while Huawei expects about $12bn of AI-chip revenue in 2026, up from $7.5bn.

flashpoints.title: Export controls against China
flashpoints.advantage: control of the chain's choke points
flashpoints.mechanism: The US and its allies deny China EUV tools and the best accelerators, so Chinese chips stay generations behind and must be made on older DUV machines.
flashpoints.outcome: SMIC makes Huawei's chips without EUV at a 5.4% foundry share, and China still bought 23% of ASML's Q3 equipment sales (about EUR 1.93bn) in older DUV tools.

flashpoints.title: Chips for equity
flashpoints.mechanism: NVIDIA invests in its customers (OpenAI, Anthropic, CoreWeave, Intel) so they can keep buying its systems, and AMD answers with warrants.
flashpoints.outcome: NVIDIA offered up to $100bn to OpenAI and up to $10bn to Anthropic, put $2bn into CoreWeave at $87.20 a share, and AMD offered OpenAI warrants for up to 160m shares.

flashpoints.title: Oracle wins OpenAI's biggest contract
flashpoints.mechanism: When Microsoft gave up exclusivity, Oracle won OpenAI's largest compute contract by building to order and carrying the cost on its own balance sheet.
flashpoints.outcome: OpenAI agreed to buy $300bn of compute from Oracle over five years, Oracle's backlog reached $664bn, and it spent $28.5bn of capex in one quarter.

flashpoints.title: Anthropic against OpenAI
flashpoints.mechanism: Anthropic sold to enterprises and developers and bought compute on three chip platforms as revenue arrived, while OpenAI built on consumer scale and very large commitments.
flashpoints.outcome: Anthropic's run-rate rose from about $9bn to over $47bn by May 2026 and its valuation ($965bn) passed OpenAI's ($852bn), whose run-rate was about $50bn in October.

flashpoints.title: Google absorbs the ChatGPT shock
flashpoints.mechanism: Google answered ChatGPT by building Gemini into its search, phones and cloud on its own TPUs, accepting the cost to its search margin rather than leaving the field to a new rival.
flashpoints.outcome: Google still held 91.05% of search in October 2026 and Gemini took 25.6% of chatbot traffic, while ChatGPT's share fell from 73.3% to 55.5% even as it reached 900 million weekly users.

flashpoints.title: Open weights against closed labs
flashpoints.mechanism: DeepSeek releases near-frontier models free under the MIT licence and runs them cheaply on Chinese chips, so closed labs must justify charging for what it gives away.
flashpoints.outcome: DeepSeek released the 1.6-trillion-parameter V4-Pro in April 2026 and was valued at $52bn in May, against Anthropic's $965bn, and Anthropic accused it of distilling Claude.

flashpoints.title: The talent auction
flashpoints.mechanism: Meta used its advertising cash to buy researchers outright, with packages reported up to $300m and a $14.3bn stake in Scale AI to hire its founder.
flashpoints.outcome: Meta Superintelligence Labs grew to about 3,000 people and its Muse Spark model reached the top five of Artificial Analysis benchmarks in July 2026.

flashpoints.title: Cash flow against leverage
flashpoints.mechanism: Microsoft funds about $170bn a year of capex from operations, while Oracle and CoreWeave borrow against their customers' contracts to build.
flashpoints.outcome: Microsoft expects to stay free-cash-flow positive, while Oracle spent $28.5bn of capex in a quarter and CoreWeave carries about $35.1bn of debt against a $25.59bn market value.

flashpoints.title: The turbine queue
flashpoints.advantage: a full order book in a scarce product
flashpoints.mechanism: Data centres need firm power faster than grids can add it, and only three firms make large gas turbines, so buyers reserve slots years ahead.
flashpoints.outcome: GE Vernova's gas backlog and slot reservations reached 122 GW, heading for at least 130 GW, and its Q3 2026 orders rose 96% to $29bn.

flashpoints.title: GLP-1: Lilly passes Novo
flashpoints.advantage: a better drug, made at volume
flashpoints.mechanism: Novo made the obesity market, but Lilly's tirzepatide worked better and Lilly scaled supply faster, so it took the growth.
flashpoints.outcome: Lilly's Q3 2026 revenue rose 39% to $24.40bn and it guides $91-92bn for the year, while Novo guides 2026 sales growth of -2% to +2%.

flashpoints.title: BYD out-builds Tesla
flashpoints.mechanism: BYD makes its own batteries and chips and builds cars at a cost Tesla cannot match, so Tesla moves its story to autonomy and robots.
flashpoints.outcome: In Q3 2026 BYD sold 762,478 battery-electric cars to Tesla's 486,532, and Tesla's operating margin fell to 2.6%, though Tesla is still valued at $1.415 trillion against BYD's $116bn.

flashpoints.title: Trainium wins Anthropic
flashpoints.advantage: its own chip sold with its cloud
flashpoints.mechanism: Amazon designs Trainium and sells it with AWS capacity, so a lab that commits to AWS gets cheaper compute and Amazon keeps the margin NVIDIA would have taken.
flashpoints.outcome: In April 2026 Anthropic committed $100bn over ten years to Trainium and Graviton (5 GW), alongside up to $25bn of new Amazon investment, while AWS grew 39% to $46.0bn a quarter.

flashpoints.title: Microsoft hedges its OpenAI bet
flashpoints.advantage: a stake in one lab, a channel for all
flashpoints.mechanism: Microsoft kept about 27% of OpenAI and a large Azure commitment while investing in Anthropic and selling Claude, so it earns whichever lab wins its enterprise customers.
flashpoints.outcome: Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9bn in a quarter, up 30%, while OpenAI placed its largest new contracts with Oracle ($300bn over five years) and AWS ($38bn).

flashpoints.title: xAI rents Colossus to a rival
flashpoints.advantage: capacity built fast, with its own power
flashpoints.mechanism: xAI built its Colossus data centres faster than rivals could find power and sites, and now rents capacity to a competing lab like a GPU landlord.
flashpoints.outcome: Anthropic pays SpaceX's xAI $1.25bn a month for Colossus 1 through May 2029, while xAI's segment lost $6.4bn on $3.2bn of revenue in 2025.

flashpoints.title: Walmart's stores against Amazon
flashpoints.advantage: stores near every shopper, and their data
flashpoints.mechanism: Walmart turned its store network into fast delivery points and its shoppers' data into an advertising business, competing with Amazon on speed and on ad margin.
flashpoints.outcome: Walmart's global advertising grew 38% in a quarter and it is the world's second-largest company by revenue, while Amazon delivered over 1.5 billion items same-day or overnight in a quarter.

flashpoints.title: Seven leave OpenAI
flashpoints.mechanism: Seven OpenAI researchers left to found Anthropic, taking their knowledge of scaling and safety with them.
flashpoints.outcome: Five years later Anthropic was valued at $965bn, above OpenAI's $852bn.

flashpoints.title: AWS leads cloud
flashpoints.mechanism: Amazon turned its internal infrastructure into the first large public cloud and kept the lead by scale.
flashpoints.outcome: AWS held 31% of cloud infrastructure in Q1 2023 against Azure's 25% and Google Cloud's 11%.

flashpoints.title: Intel leaves DRAM
flashpoints.advantage: giving up a lost market in time
flashpoints.mechanism: When Japanese memory makers crushed DRAM margins, Intel moved its capital to the microprocessor that the PC market needed.
flashpoints.outcome: Grove took Intel out of memory, and the 386 made Intel the key supplier of the PC standard.

flashpoints.title: Meta buys its challengers
flashpoints.advantage: cash from a network buys the next network
flashpoints.mechanism: Facebook bought the young networks that could have replaced it before they grew large.
flashpoints.outcome: Instagram for about $1bn in 2012 and WhatsApp for $19bn in 2014.

flashpoints.title: The eight leave Shockley
flashpoints.mechanism: A founder who could recruit but not manage lost his whole team, who took the technique with them.
flashpoints.outcome: Fairchild formed 18 Sept 1957; Shockley's firm was acquired by Clevite.

flashpoints.title: Planar monolithic IC against Kilby's version
flashpoints.mechanism: Photo-masked planar fabrication turned the IC from a lab result into a product.
flashpoints.outcome: Noyce's monolithic IC, 1959; Kilby later won the Nobel Prize.

flashpoints.title: The IBM PC adopts Intel
flashpoints.advantage: a standard set by an open design
flashpoints.mechanism: IBM's open architecture let clones copy the PC but not the chip, so the standard's value went to Intel and Microsoft.
flashpoints.outcome: Compaq's 1986 386 machine beat IBM to market and made Intel the key supplier.

flashpoints.title: Nvidia buys 3dfx
flashpoints.mechanism: After the GeForce 256, the one-time leader in consumer 3D lost ground and sold its assets.
flashpoints.outcome: Nvidia agreed in Dec 2000 to acquire 3dfx's intellectual assets.

flashpoints.title: AlexNet on two gaming GPUs
flashpoints.advantage: parallel hardware already in the market
flashpoints.mechanism: A deep network trained in 5 to 6 days on two $500 GPUs beat every other ImageNet entry, showing that GPUs, not CPUs, were the engine of deep learning.
flashpoints.outcome: Won ImageNet 2012; CUDA (2007) was the ready software.

flashpoints.title: ChatGPT
flashpoints.advantage: betting on scale and shipping first
flashpoints.mechanism: OpenAI turned scaling laws and GPT-3 into a product the public could use.
flashpoints.outcome: 100 million monthly users in two months; 900 million weekly in February 2026.

flashpoints.title: The state breaks Standard Oil
flashpoints.mechanism: Standard Oil's share fell from 91% to 64% as rivals grew, and the courts ordered it broken up.
flashpoints.outcome: Share 91% in 1904, 64% in 1911, then dissolution.

flashpoints.title: Ford's moving assembly line
flashpoints.mechanism: The moving line at Highland Park made the car affordable to the middle class, until GM sold brands and credit.
flashpoints.outcome: The Model T sold in millions over nearly two decades; GM later held first place for 77 years.

flashpoints.title: IBM's mainframe lock-in
flashpoints.mechanism: System/360 made a compatible family customers could not leave; IBM made 80% of US computers.
flashpoints.outcome: 80% of US and 70% of world computers in the 1960s-1970s; an $8 billion loss in 1993.

flashpoints.title: Apple sees the GUI at PARC
flashpoints.mechanism: Xerox let Apple see the Alto in exchange for stock options; Apple built the mass-market GUI.
flashpoints.outcome: Apple released the first mass-market GUI computers.

flashpoints.title: The PC clones and MS-DOS
flashpoints.mechanism: IBM used an outside operating system and an open design, so clones could copy the PC and only Microsoft kept control.
flashpoints.outcome: More than 90% of US workplace PC users on MS-DOS; IBM's $8 billion loss in 1993.

flashpoints.title: The Bell System is broken up
flashpoints.mechanism: AT&T settled the antitrust suit by giving up its 24 local companies, keeping long distance, Western Electric and Bell Labs.
flashpoints.outcome: Divestiture effective 1 January 1984.

flashpoints.title: Walmart passes Sears
flashpoints.mechanism: Walmart's profit lead over Kmart and Sears by the late 1980s led to the largest revenue by October 1989; Sears sold off assets and went bankrupt in 2018.
flashpoints.outcome: Largest retailer from 1989; Sears bankrupt October 2018.

flashpoints.title: Fuji's price war on Kodak
flashpoints.mechanism: Fuji cut price and marketed aggressively, taking Kodak's film share before digital made film shrink.
flashpoints.outcome: Fuji's US film share 10% to 17%; Kodak Chapter 11 in January 2012.

flashpoints.title: US v. Microsoft
flashpoints.mechanism: The court found monopolisation and tying and ordered a breakup in June 2000; the remedy was an ordered breakup.
flashpoints.outcome: Judgment 3 April 2000, breakup order 7 June 2000.

flashpoints.title: Yahoo declines Google
flashpoints.mechanism: Yahoo declined to buy Google for 1 million dollars in 1998 and rejected Yahoo's final 3 billion dollar offer in 2002; Google's search won.
flashpoints.outcome: Google 91.05% of search in October 2026; Yahoo 1.18%.

flashpoints.title: Netflix beats Blockbuster
flashpoints.mechanism: Blockbuster declined to buy Netflix for 50 million dollars in 2000 and filed for Chapter 11 in 2010 with 900 million dollars of debt.
flashpoints.outcome: From 9,094 stores in 2004 to bankruptcy in 2010.

flashpoints.title: The iPhone against Nokia and BlackBerry
flashpoints.mechanism: Nokia held 40.4% of handsets in Q4 2007, then turned to Windows Phone in 2011; BlackBerry fell from 85 million to 23 million subscribers.
flashpoints.outcome: iOS holds 27.61% and Android 72.36% of mobile OS use; Windows 0%.

flashpoints.title: Toyota passes GM
flashpoints.mechanism: Toyota's production system gave lower cost and fewer defects; GM lost the world title after 77 years and took a bailout.
flashpoints.outcome: GM bailouts of 17.4 billion dollars by March 2009.

flashpoints.title: Huawei passes Ericsson
flashpoints.mechanism: State-backed scale made Huawei the largest telecom equipment maker.
flashpoints.outcome: Largest telecom equipment maker from 2012.

flashpoints.title: The steppe system against walled cities
flashpoints.mechanism: Rider mobility took the field; captured engineers and prisoners took the walls.
flashpoints.outcome: By 1227 the empire ran from the Pacific to the Caspian, the largest contiguous state in history.

flashpoints.title: Gaugamela
flashpoints.advantage: pike line plus a cavalry wedge
flashpoints.mechanism: Cavalry drew Persian horse to the flanks and the wedge struck the centre.
flashpoints.outcome: A heavily outnumbered Macedonian army won; the Achaemenid empire broke.

flashpoints.title: Jena and Auerstedt
flashpoints.mechanism: Corps marched apart and fought together, with artillery spearheading.
flashpoints.outcome: The Prussian army was broken on 14 October 1806.

flashpoints.title: The coalitions restore the balance
flashpoints.mechanism: Austria, Prussia, Russia and Britain acted together after 1813.
flashpoints.outcome: Leipzig (1813) and Waterloo (1815); the Vienna settlement kept a balance of powers until 1914.

flashpoints.title: Industrial weight decides the Second World War
flashpoints.advantage: oil, coal and steel on the Allied side
flashpoints.mechanism: Allied output dwarfed Axis output; the US supplied two thirds of Allied munitions.
flashpoints.outcome: Allied crude oil was 1,043,000,000 tonnes against 66,000,000.

flashpoints.title: Bretton Woods
flashpoints.advantage: control of the world's gold and the dollar
flashpoints.mechanism: The dollar became the anchor of a 44-country order.
flashpoints.outcome: The US held two thirds of the world's gold; by 1950 it had 27.3 percent of world economic activity.

flashpoints.title: The end-Cretaceous extinction
flashpoints.mechanism: Animals that could shelter and eat little outlived the impact winter.
flashpoints.outcome: About 75% of species died; non-avian dinosaurs could not shelter, mammal lineages survived with losses.

flashpoints.title: The predator-prey cycle
flashpoints.mechanism: Predator numbers follow prey numbers; the cycle repeats.
flashpoints.outcome: Lynx rise and fall with hare, in Alaska and central Canada.

flashpoints.title: Meta moves a $27bn campus off its balance sheet
flashpoints.mechanism: Blue Owl funds own 80% of the venture, a bond priced at 6.581% funds it, and Meta leases the campus and guarantees its value for 16 years.
flashpoints.outcome: $27.3bn bond; Meta received about $3bn; a second 80/20 venture followed with BlackRock in July 2026.

flashpoints.title: SpaceX turns its listing into a data-centre war chest
flashpoints.mechanism: An IPO, then a debut bond of at least $20bn, then tenant contracts, fund a build the estimate puts at 1.7 GW now and 13 GW by 2027.
flashpoints.outcome: Reflection pays $150m a month; Anthropic and Google contracts reach $26bn a year but can be cancelled in 90 days.

flashpoints.title: Oracle borrows to build for a single customer
flashpoints.mechanism: A record $38bn loan to Vantage funds campuses Oracle leases for OpenAI, on top of $117.7bn of borrowings on its own balance sheet.
flashpoints.outcome: Rating one notch above junk after a July downgrade; lenders sell loan pieces at a discount.

flashpoints.title: A neocloud buys power with debt
flashpoints.mechanism: Contracted power rose from 3.7 GW to 4.2 GW in six weeks, financed by a $3.1bn syndicated loan, over $10bn of unsecured debt and a $1bn strategic stake.
flashpoints.outcome: Property and equipment grew from $30.6bn to $46.7bn in six months; short contracts now price at about $40m per MW.

flashpoints.title: Control without ownership
flashpoints.mechanism: Dual-class shares give a founder the vote while the public supplies the capital.
flashpoints.outcome: Zuckerberg holds about 61% of Meta's votes on about 13% of the shares; Page and Brin hold 52.7% of Alphabet's votes; Musk holds more than 82% of SpaceX's.

flashpoints.title: OpenAI's recapitalisation
flashpoints.advantage: capital and compute traded for a stake
flashpoints.mechanism: The nonprofit kept control while Microsoft, the compute supplier, converted its funding into a 27% stake.
flashpoints.outcome: Foundation 26%, Microsoft about 27%, investors and employees 47%.

flashpoints.title: The supplier owns its customers
flashpoints.advantage: a high share price turned into equity in customers
flashpoints.mechanism: NVIDIA invests in the labs and neoclouds that buy its GPUs, so demand and ownership rise together.
flashpoints.outcome: NVIDIA put $30bn into OpenAI, owns 10.29% of CoreWeave and a stake in Intel now worth more than $25bn.

flashpoints.title: Two clouds, one lab
flashpoints.mechanism: Anthropic took money from both rivals but capped their stakes and issues them non-voting shares.
flashpoints.outcome: Amazon capped at 12%, Google at 14.99%.

flashpoints.title: Stock buys the rival before it grows
flashpoints.advantage: a rising share price as currency
flashpoints.mechanism: Facebook paid about $1bn in cash and stock for a photo app before it could become a rival network.
flashpoints.outcome: Instagram, bought at $1bn, joined Meta; WhatsApp followed in 2014 at $19.3bn, 79% paid in stock and restricted stock.

flashpoints.title: $15bn of shares for a messenger
flashpoints.mechanism: $12bn in Facebook shares plus $3bn of restricted stock units, retaining WhatsApp staff, bought the most popular messenger out of the market.
flashpoints.outcome: A $19.3bn price, largest deal to date; the messenger now has billions of users inside Meta.

flashpoints.title: Licence-and-hire: buying talent without buying the company
flashpoints.advantage: cash pile and share price to outbid for founders
flashpoints.mechanism: Google paid about $2.7bn for Character.AI talent and $2.4bn for Windsurf leaders, taking them after OpenAI's $3bn bid fell apart.
flashpoints.outcome: The startups remained legally independent, so the deals avoided a merger review; Microsoft had used the same structure for Inflection at $650m.

flashpoints.title: Meta pays for a lab
flashpoints.advantage: share price funds pay no start-up can match
flashpoints.mechanism: Meta bought a stake in Scale AI for $14.3bn, hired its CEO, and offered researchers packages up to $300m over four years.
flashpoints.outcome: Altman said none of OpenAI's best accepted; at least ten offers went to OpenAI staff. Meta's pay in stock rests on its own share price.

flashpoints.title: The market punishes the loss-funded bet
flashpoints.advantage: ad profits funding a VR land grab
flashpoints.mechanism: Reality Labs lost billions a year, funded by the ad business; when profit declined the share price fell 27%.
flashpoints.outcome: About $230bn of value gone in a day; Reality Labs has lost $80bn since 2020 and Meta still expects $18-19bn of loss in 2026.

flashpoints.title: The biggest company in the world, then 431bn lost
flashpoints.advantage: a stock price high enough to buy a whole sector
flashpoints.mechanism: At the dot-com peak Cisco was worth over $500bn and paid for acquisitions with richly priced shares.
flashpoints.outcome: The bubble burst: $431bn of value lost; the Nasdaq fell 78% by October 2002.

flashpoints.title: 47bn of valuation, then bankruptcy
flashpoints.mechanism: WeWork raised $12.8bn at valuations up to $47bn and grew faster than its leases could earn.
flashpoints.outcome: The IPO was cancelled in 2019; it listed by SPAC in 2021 and filed for Chapter 11 on 6 November 2023, with SoftBank affiliates taking 20% of the reorganised firm.

flashpoints.title: Shares fold a loss-making lab into a profitable rocket firm
flashpoints.advantage: an all-stock merger at a 1.25 trillion valuation
flashpoints.mechanism: SpaceX swapped its own shares for xAI at a negotiated mark, tying the lab's compute needs to the parent's balance sheet and a coming IPO.
flashpoints.outcome: A combined entity valued at about $1.25 trillion; SpaceX listed in June 2026 at $135 a share.

flashpoints.title: Losses funded by a valuation
flashpoints.advantage: investor belief funds a burn that exceeds revenue
flashpoints.mechanism: OpenAI burned $3.7bn in Q1 2026 on $5.7bn of revenue and forecasts $278bn of cash burn to 2030, all funded by investors and partners who trade capital for compute demand.
flashpoints.outcome: The strategy works while capital stays cheap; if funding stops the burn cannot be sustained, which is how WeWork and FTX ended.

flashpoints.title: NVIDIA takes out an inference rival
flashpoints.advantage: a cash pile that can buy a competitor's leaders
flashpoints.mechanism: NVIDIA licensed Groq's technology and took its founder and engineers; CNBC put the deal at $20bn in cash, three times Groq's last valuation of $6.9bn.
flashpoints.outcome: Groq stays nominally independent; the rival's team now works for the incumbent. The $20bn figure is reported, not confirmed.

scenarios.title: Compounding demand
scenarios.premise: Suppose AI revenue keeps pace with spending: the leading labs' combined revenue run-rate more than doubles from about $100bn in late 2026 to over $200bn by the end of 2027 and the clouds' AI revenue grows 40% or more a year, so the hyperscalers raise capex from about $725-828bn in 2026 to over $1 trillion in 2027 and keep raising it through 2028, with chips, memory, packaging and power staying sold out.
signposts: The labs' combined run-rate passing $150bn during 2027
Hyperscalers guiding 2027 capex above $1 trillion
NVIDIA's data-centre revenue still rising quarter on quarter
HBM and CoWoS lead times lengthening rather than shortening
scenarios.reading: The scarcest inputs win most: ASML, TSMC, memory, power and NVIDIA keep pricing power, and the clouds earn back their capex. The labs grow in absolute terms but not against each other, since all of them ride the same wave. No one in the chain loses outright; the losers are relative, firms outside it that lose capital and attention.

scenarios.title: Capex digestion
scenarios.premise: Suppose AI revenue disappoints in 2027: the labs' run-rate growth slows to under 30% a year and enterprises cut pilots, so the hyperscalers cut capex by 30-40% from the 2026 level of about $725-828bn and hold it there for at least 18 months, as in past telecom and memory busts, while the Fed keeps rates near 4% and credit for data-centre builders tightens.
signposts: A hyperscaler cutting its 2027 capex guidance
GPU rental prices and HBM contract prices falling
Neocloud refinancing stress: CoreWeave's and Oracle's borrowing costs
Memory-maker shares falling on record earnings (SK Hynix fell 18.8% from 1 September 2026)
scenarios.reading: The scarcity premium reverses: the leveraged builders (CoreWeave, Oracle) and the labs with the largest commitments fall first, then memory and NVIDIA, whose $279bn of purchase commitments and customer financing become liabilities, and SoftBank with them. Cash-rich holders such as Berkshire gain the chance to buy; Apple, Visa, Walmart and Lilly are barely touched, and buyers get cheaper compute.

scenarios.title: The power wall
scenarios.premise: Suppose electricity, not chips or money, becomes the binding limit: grid connections in the main US markets take four years or more, large gas turbines are sold out to 2030 and the Hormuz disruption keeps gas and power prices high, so new data-centre capacity comes online 30-50% slower than planned through 2028 and firms that already own powered sites or their own generation are the only ones that can grow on schedule.
signposts: GE Vernova's gas backlog passing 130 GW, with delivery slots beyond 2030
Grid-connection waits for data centres in Virginia, Texas and Arizona
Wholesale power prices near data-centre clusters
Hyperscalers buying power plants or building their own generation
scenarios.reading: Advantage moves from chips to watts: nuclear owners (Constellation), turbine makers and whoever already holds powered capacity gain, including xAI, whose Colossus has its own power, and Berkshire through its utilities. Labs and GPU landlords that must buy new capacity lose time that money cannot buy back, and the server builders sell fewer racks.

scenarios.title: Taiwan disruption
scenarios.premise: Suppose a Chinese blockade or quarantine of Taiwan in 2027 halts most of TSMC's Taiwan output for six months or more: most of the world's leading-edge logic and advanced packaging stops, shipping and insurance to Taiwan freeze, and no other foundry can replace the lost volume for several years.
signposts: Chinese military exercises around Taiwan and war-risk insurance for shipping
The ramp of TSMC's fabs in Arizona and Japan
Intel's 18A and 14A winning outside customers
Governments stockpiling chips and packaging capacity
scenarios.reading: Everyone above TSMC loses, NVIDIA and Apple most, because the choke point has no substitute for years. Intel and Samsung gain as the only other leading-edge fabs, and China's own stack (SMIC, Huawei) gains relative ground. Firms that hold inventory or own their workloads survive; leveraged buyers of compute are in danger.

scenarios.title: Models commoditised
scenarios.premise: Suppose open-weight models (DeepSeek, Qwen and others) match each new frontier model within a few months and are served at a tenth of the price or less from 2027, while the closed labs' prices per token fall 70-90% a year, so model makers lose pricing power even though total use of AI keeps growing.
signposts: Open-weight models' benchmark scores against the frontier
The price per million tokens of the leading APIs
The labs' gross margins and enterprise churn
Usage share of Chinese open models outside China
scenarios.reading: The model stops being the toll-gate: DeepSeek and China's open-model ecosystem gain, and so do the buyers and firms that use AI rather than sell it. The closed labs and their financiers lose pricing power, and the GPU landlords that depend on them lose contracts. The big clouds and Apple are little changed: they sell whatever model wins.

scenarios.title: Regulatory clampdown
scenarios.premise: Suppose the US, the EU and several US states impose binding AI rules from 2027 (licensing and audits of frontier models, liability for harms, limits on training data and on data-centre power use) and antitrust remedies force the largest platforms to separate parts of their search, advertising, app-store or AI businesses, so frontier development slows and compliance costs billions a year.
signposts: Fines and obligations under the EU AI Act for general-purpose models
US federal or state bills licensing frontier models
Remedies in the US search and advertising antitrust cases
Moratoria or power-use rules for new data centres
scenarios.reading: Western rules and remedies slow the Western frontier: Alphabet, Meta, OpenAI and Microsoft face the costs and the break-ups, and the chain that sells to them slows. Labs outside the rules (DeepSeek, China) gain relative ground, as does Palantir, already built for government compliance.

scenarios.title: US-China decoupling
scenarios.premise: Suppose the US and China cut technology trade almost entirely from 2027 for at least three years: no US or allied chips, chipmaking tools, servicing, design software or cloud services sold to China; China bans US AI chips and restricts exports of rare earths and other critical minerals; and new legislation reimposes broad tariffs on Chinese goods.
signposts: New US rules on DUV servicing and memory-making tools
China's licences for rare-earth exports
Apple's and Tesla's sales in China
Huawei's Ascend shipments and SMIC's capacity
scenarios.reading: A full cutoff of tools and servicing hurts China's fabs (SMIC, CXMT) more than protection helps them, at least for two or three years, while Huawei holds. Firms that build or sell across the line (Apple, Foxconn, Tencent, BYD abroad) lose; Intel and TSMC gain as the West's fabs. Western toolmakers lose revenue but not position, and NVIDIA has already lost China.

scenarios.title: The market turns
scenarios.premise: Suppose that in 2027 the stock market turns as it did in 2000-2002: over 2027 and 2028 the price-to-earnings multiples of the most expensive companies fall by half or more, the equity window for loss-making companies closes for about 18 months, credit spreads widen and buybacks stop, while demand for AI keeps growing, but more slowly, at 20-30% a year.
signposts: Loss-making listings and late-stage private rounds pulled or repriced
Buyback authorisations suspended
Credit spreads on data-centre debt widening
The share of the S&P 500 in its ten largest companies falling
scenarios.reading: The share price stops working as a weapon. Companies that paid for growth with their valuation (the labs, SpaceX and xAI, CoreWeave, the richest multiples) must cut or sell themselves; those that fund themselves from profits (Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Berkshire, Walmart) buy what the others cannot afford, and the few end the bust holding more of the market than before. Written by the lead as an eighth world, after a critic noted that none of the seven closed the equity window.

labs-microsoft-capex-fy27.claim: Microsoft expects around $170 billion of capital spending for the year and more than $50 billion in the second quarter.

labs-microsoft-capex-q1.claim: Microsoft spent around $45 billion on capital expenditures in fiscal Q1 2027 and expects more than $50 billion in the second.

labs-alphabet-capex-2026.claim: Alphabet raised its 2026 capex guide to $195-205 billion and signalled 2027 capex above $300 billion.
labs-alphabet-capex-2026.quote: Alphabet raised its FY26 capex guide to $195B-$205B and signaled 2027 capex will top $300B.

labs-alphabet-capex-q3.claim: Alphabet's Q3 2026 capital expenditures were $51.4 billion against $24.0 billion a year earlier.
labs-alphabet-capex-q3.quote: Purchases of property and equipment, Alphabet’s capital expenditures, reached $51.4 billion in the quarter, against $24.0 billion a year earlier.

labs-google-cloud-q3.claim: Google Cloud revenue doubled to $30.7 billion in Q3 2026, with capex $51.4 billion.
labs-google-cloud-q3.quote: The key insight: Alphabet’s capital expenditures of $51.4 billion exceeded its $42.3 billion of operating cash flow in the third quarter, while Google Cloud revenue doubled to $30.7 billion, according to the release.

labs-amazon-capex-2026.claim: Amazon expects 2026 cash capital expenditures of approximately $220 billion.
labs-amazon-capex-2026.quote: In the same release, Amazon said it continues to expect 2026 cash capital expenditures of “approximately $220 billion”.

labs-amazon-capex-q3.claim: Amazon's Q3 2026 purchases of property and equipment were $77.3 billion.
labs-amazon-capex-q3.quote: By our arithmetic, that leaves about $44.3 billion for the fourth quarter, after $77.3 billion in the third.

labs-meta-capex-2026.claim: Meta narrowed its 2026 capital expenditure outlook to $135-145 billion.
labs-meta-capex-2026.quote: Meta reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $64.6 billion, up 26% from a year earlier, and narrowed its full-year capital-expenditure outlook to $135 billion-$145 billion.

labs-meta-capex-q3.claim: Meta's capital expenditures, including finance-lease principal, were $34.9 billion in Q3 2026.
labs-meta-capex-q3.quote: The company said capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases, were $34.9 billion in the September quarter.

labs-oracle-rpo.claim: Oracle books $664 billion in remaining performance obligations.
labs-oracle-rpo.quote: Oracle books $664 billion in remaining performance obligations while confirming its newest contracts do not enlarge its capital plan.

labs-oracle-capex-q1.claim: Oracle spent $28.5 billion on capex in a single fiscal quarter.
labs-oracle-capex-q1.quote: Oracle’s own disclosure demonstrates the limit of that strategy: at some point, somebody holds the capex, and this quarter Oracle held $28.5 billion of it.

labs-oracle-capex-fy27.claim: Oracle expects $70 billion of its own capital spending in fiscal 2027, plus $20-25 billion repaid by customers.

labs-microsoft-openai-stake.claim: Microsoft holds about $135 billion of OpenAI Group PBC, roughly 27 percent, and OpenAI contracted to buy an incremental $250 billion of Azure.

labs-openai-nvidia-100bn.claim: NVIDIA intends to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI progressively as each gigawatt of NVIDIA systems is deployed.
labs-openai-nvidia-100bn.quote: To support the partnership, NVIDIA intends to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI progressively as each gigawatt is deployed.

labs-openai-amd-warrant.claim: AMD issued OpenAI a warrant for up to 160 million AMD shares, vesting as purchases scale up to 6 gigawatts.
labs-openai-amd-warrant.quote: As part of the agreement, to further align strategic interests, AMD has issued OpenAI a warrant for up to 160 million shares of AMD common stock, structured to vest as specific milestones are achieved.

labs-openai-broadcom-10gw.claim: OpenAI and Broadcom will co-develop and deploy 10 gigawatts of accelerators and network systems.
labs-openai-broadcom-10gw.quote: “OpenAI has been in the forefront of the AI revolution since the ChatGPT moment, and we are thrilled to co-develop and deploy 10 gigawatts of next- generation accelerators and network systems to pave the way for the future of AI.”

labs-openai-oracle-300bn.claim: OpenAI agreed to buy $300 billion of computing power from Oracle over five years, per the Wall Street Journal.
labs-openai-oracle-300bn.quote: OpenAI established a partnership with Oracle, signing off on an agreement to buy $300 billion in computing power over a five-year period, according to reporting by The Wall Street Journal.

labs-openai-aws-38bn.claim: OpenAI will rent $38 billion of cloud infrastructure from AWS in a seven-year partnership.
labs-openai-aws-38bn.quote: OpenAI Group PBC will rent $38 billion worth of cloud infrastructure from Amazon Web Services Inc. as part of a seven-year partnership announced today.

labs-openai-coreweave-22bn.claim: CoreWeave signed a $22.4 billion deal with OpenAI for dedicated compute capacity.
labs-openai-coreweave-22bn.quote: CoreWeave CoreWeave, a specialist AI cloud provider known for its high-performance GPU infrastructure, signed a $22.4 billion deal with OpenAI to deliver dedicated compute capacity.

labs-softbank-openai-total.claim: SoftBank completed its final payment, taking its cumulative investment in OpenAI to $64.6 billion (2 October 2026).
labs-softbank-openai-total.quote: SoftBank Group announced on October 2 that it had completed its final payment for an additional investment in OpenAI, taking its cumulative investment in the AI company to $64.6 billion.

labs-stargate-500bn.claim: Stargate, the OpenAI, SoftBank, Oracle and MGX joint venture, plans to spend up to $500 billion on US AI infrastructure by 2029.
labs-stargate-500bn.quote: The venture plans to spend up to US$500 billion to build AI infrastructure in the United States by 2029.

labs-anthropic-azure-nvidia.claim: Anthropic committed to purchase $30 billion of Azure compute, and NVIDIA and Microsoft committed to invest up to $10 billion and $5 billion in Anthropic.
labs-anthropic-azure-nvidia.quote: Anthropic has committed to purchase $30 billion of Azure compute capacity and to contract additional compute capacity up to one gigawatt.

labs-anthropic-google-tpu.claim: Anthropic plans to use up to one million Google TPUs, worth tens of billions of dollars and well over a gigawatt in 2026.

labs-anthropic-broadcom-tpu.claim: Broadcom disclosed it will supply Anthropic with roughly 3.5 gigawatts of Google TPU capacity starting in 2027.

labs-zuckerberg-misspend.claim: Zuckerberg on the record: Meta might misspend a couple hundred billion dollars, but the risk is higher on the other side.
labs-zuckerberg-misspend.quote: “If we end up misspending a couple hundred billion dollars, that’s going to be very unfortunate obviously. But I would say the risk is higher on the other side,” Zuckerberg said.

labs-pichai-irrationality.claim: Pichai on the record: there is some irrationality in the AI boom and no company, Google included, would be immune if it bursts.
labs-pichai-irrationality.quote: "No company is going to be immune, including us."

labs-amodei-bankrupt.claim: Amodei on the record: if revenue is only $800 billion rather than $1 trillion, no hedge could stop him going bankrupt if he bought that much compute.
labs-amodei-bankrupt.quote: “If my revenue is not $1 trillion, if it’s even $800 billion, there’s no force on Earth, there’s no hedge on Earth that could stop me from going bankrupt if I buy that much compute,”
